newsitem.title: USA: U.S. okays $400 mln loan for Calif. rail project.
newsitem.headline: U.S. okays $400 mln loan for Calif. rail project.

text.p: Federal transportation officials on Friday finalized a $400 million loan agreement for the Alameda Corridor project, a $1.9 billion Los Angeles-to-San Pedro Bay intermodal transportation system.
The mayors of Los Angeles and Long Beach hailed the move.

"The Alameda Corridor is the heart of our region's economic health for the 21st century," Los Angeles Mayor Richard Riordan said in a statement. "It will mean tens of thousands of quality jobs for Angelenos, and it will secure southern California's place as the country's international trade hub."
Long Beach Mayor Beverly O'Neill said the corridor would help to move Long Beach from a military-based economy to an economy focused on international trade and transportation.

The Department of Transportation said it would loan the Alameda Corridor Transportation Authority $400 million to help build the corridor, designed to improve rail operations linking the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach to shippers throughout North America. The department said it would distribute the loan funds over three years beginning in 1997.
The Alameda Corridor Transportation Authority would repay the department with corridor fees and port contributions.
The loan must be repaid within 30 years, officials said.

The ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach currently handle one-fourth of all U.S. waterborne international trade and are linked to 2.5 million jobs. The ports handle over $116 billion of trade each year, California state officials estimated.

Construction of the Alameda Corridor project began in 1994 and is scheduled to be completed by 2001. The project is expected to create about 10,000 local, construction-related jobs. With the transportation corridor in place, the amount of goods traveling through the ports would increase to $253 billion, state officials estimated.

"By taking this step today, President Clinton is acknowledging California's preeminence as America's gateway to the vast and emerging markets in the Pacific Rim and the integral role the Los Angeles-Long Beach Port complex plays in our continued export growth," Gov. Pete Wilson said.
The Department of Transportation's Federal Highway Administration and Federal Railroad Administration completed an environmental review of the project in May 1996.

In addition to the $400 million loan, the project will be financed with $400 million from the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, $700 million from project revenue bonds and $350 million from state and local sources.
